passage: Last month our class made a rule together: no copying homework, even from friends. We all signed the chart. The next week Damini, my bench partner, asked for my maths notebook before the bell. "Just the last sum, please, Tanuja." I said no. She sulked all morning. But when Ma'am checked, and three boys got caught copying, she looked at our row and said, "Thank you for keeping our class promise." My chest felt big and warm. I'd done what we all agreed. Honestly, I felt a bit too pleased with myself when the boys got scolded. Damini talked to me again by lunch.

qa.q: What did the class sign?
qa.a: A chart with the rule of no copying homework.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja's chest feel "big and warm"?
qa.a: Tanuja felt proud and validated for keeping the rule the whole class had agreed on, especially when Ma'am thanked their row.

qa.q: What could Tanuja watch out for about feeling "too pleased" when others got scolded?
qa.a: Keeping a rule is good, but enjoying others' trouble can slide into looking down on them.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt when Tanuja said no?
qa.a: Annoyed and let down at first, which is why she sulked, but she seemed to get over it by lunch.

grounding: It shows a child feeling validated for keeping a rule her class made together, with a hint of smugness.

passage: Games teacher's note, Anjali. In today's inter-house throwball match, the ball touched Uma's fingers before going out, but the umpire gave the point to her team. Uma raised her hand. "Ma'am, it touched me. It's their point." Her team groaned. She stood straight, chin up, and said, "We made the fair-play pledge." They lost by one point. Afterwards she walked around with her head high, telling everyone the pledge mattered more. A few teammates were still sulking. I spoke to the whole team about fair play, and about not lecturing each other.

qa.q: What did Uma tell the umpire?
qa.a: That the ball touched her, so it was the other team's point.

qa.q: What does Uma walking around with her head high after losing suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud and in the right for keeping the fair-play pledge, and that feeling mattered more to her than winning.

qa.q: Why did Anjali also talk about not lecturing each other?
qa.a: Uma's honesty was good, but telling everyone the pledge mattered more could leave teammates feeling judged.

qa.q: How might Uma's teammates feel after losing by one point?
qa.a: Some are upset because her honesty cost them the match, even if they respect the pledge.

grounding: It shows a girl feeling validated by upholding her team's fair-play pledge even at a cost.

passage:
Diary, Saturday.
Clean-up drive in the colony park today. Our Green Club made a rule: whatever you bring, you take back. Karthik threw his chips packet behind the bench. I picked it up, walked over and handed it back to him in front of everyone. "Club rule," I said. He went red and put it in his pocket. The club secretary gave me a thumbs up and said, "Well done, Reena." I felt like a real member, like I was protecting something that belonged to all of us. Maybe I could have said it more quietly, though. Karthik didn't sit with us after.

qa.q: What rule did the Green Club make?
qa.a: Whatever you bring, you take back.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after handing the packet back?
qa.a: Reena felt right and proud, like a true member protecting something shared, though later wondered about the way it was done.

qa.q: What could Reena try next time to uphold the rule without shaming anyone?
qa.a: Remind Karthik quietly or hand him a bag, so he can fix it without an audience.

qa.q: How might Karthik have experienced being corrected in front of everyone?
qa.a: Embarrassed, which may be why he didn't sit with the club afterwards.

grounding: It shows a child feeling validated as a group member by enforcing the club's shared rule.

passage: At the village school, sweets were given out after the Republic Day flag hoisting. The rule was one each. Vasudha's cousin slipped into the queue twice. Vidya saw and stayed in her place. When she got to the front, the teacher gave her one sweet and said, 'Good, Vidya, you didn't push.' Vidya stood straighter. On the walk home, Vasudha said, 'You could have taken two.' Vidya shook her head. 'Everyone agreed one each. It's right.' She felt good and warm inside.

qa.q: What was the rule for sweets after the flag hoisting?
qa.a: The rule was one each.

qa.q: Why did Vidya feel good and warm inside?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated for keeping the rule everyone had agreed to.

qa.q: What might Vidya do if someone keeps breaking the rule?
qa.a: She could tell the teacher calmly so the rule stays fair for everyone.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Vidya's choice?
qa.a: Vasudha might think Vidya was too strict, or Vasudha might quietly respect Vidya for sticking to the rule.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling validated by upholding shared rules, in a village school.

passage: In Wei's classroom in Warsaw, Olga had made a rule chart for recycling: paper, plastic, other. Some kids just threw everything in any bin. Wei always sorted his carefully, even peeling the plastic window off his lunch envelope. On Friday, Olga announced, 'Our class had the cleanest bins in school!' and put a star next to Wei's name. Wei felt his cheeks warm. At break he told a boy tossing a bottle in the paper bin, 'That goes there. We all agreed.'

qa.q: What did Wei peel off his lunch envelope?
qa.a: He peeled off the plastic window.

qa.q: What does Wei's warm cheeks when Olga put a star suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud and validated for following the class's shared rule.

qa.q: How could Wei remind others without sounding bossy?
qa.a: He could explain the reason kindly or offer to show them, instead of just correcting.

qa.q: How might the boy tossing the bottle see Wei's comment?
qa.a: He might feel a little annoyed at being corrected, or embarrassed and more careful.

grounding: Shows a child feeling righteous and validated by upholding a class's shared rule, in Poland.

passage: At the school library, the rule was simple: one book at a time, and you queue. Deepak, eleven, was third in line when a Class 7 boy walked straight to the counter. Deepak stepped out. "There's a queue." The boy rolled his eyes. The librarian, Urmila Ma'am, looked up. "Deepak's right. Back of the line, please." The boy went. Deepak felt his chest swell. Later, he told his friends three times how he'd stood up for the rules.

qa.q: What was the rule at the library?
qa.a: One book at a time, and you queue.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Urmila Ma'am backed him?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated for upholding the rule everyone shared.

qa.q: What would you advise Deepak about telling the story three times?
qa.a: It's fine to feel proud, but he could stop there so he doesn't seem to be showing off.

qa.q: How might the Class 7 boy see Deepak?
qa.a: Probably as annoying or a goody-goody, at least at first.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated by upholding a shared queue rule and being backed by an adult.

passage: I'm Trisha, and my brother Hemant, ten, became class monitor this term. At PE, the captains always picked their friends first. Hemant said, "Rule is: we count off, one-two, one-two." Some boys groaned, but the teacher agreed. The teams were even, and the match was close. Afterwards Hemant told us at dinner, "Everyone played properly for once." He was smiling all evening. I'm not sure if he was proud of the rule or of being monitor, but he seemed very sure he had done the right thing.

qa.q: How did Hemant say teams should be picked?
qa.a: By counting off, one-two, one-two.

qa.q: What might Hemant have felt at dinner?
qa.a: He seemed proud and satisfied that his fair rule worked.

qa.q: How could Hemant handle the boys who groaned?
qa.a: Explain that the rule gives everyone a fair chance, and keep applying it the same way for all.

qa.q: How does Trisha see Hemant's smile?
qa.a: Trisha wonders whether it is pride in the rule or in being monitor, but sees he feels sure he was right.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated by enforcing a fair rule for his class, seen by his sister.

passage: Monday: in Class 7, Uma found a pencil box on the floor with money inside and handed it to the teacher, because that was the class rule. Everyone clapped. She felt warm all day. Thursday: in a game of kho-kho, Hrithik broke the rule by crossing early. Uma called it out loudly. He argued, but the group backed her. Next Monday: when a friend broke a small rule, Uma scolded her in front of everyone, and the friend cried. Uma felt the warm feeling turn uneasy.

qa.q: What did Uma find on the floor?
qa.a: A pencil box with money inside.

qa.q: Why did Uma's warm feeling turn uneasy on Monday?
qa.a: She began to feel guilty that her rule-keeping had hurt a friend, not just kept things fair.

qa.q: What would you advise Uma for next time?
qa.a: Point out small rule-breaking kindly and privately, so fairness doesn't turn into shaming.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Uma after the kho-kho game?
qa.a: He may feel annoyed and see her as strict, even if the group agreed with her.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated by upholding group rules over a week, then noticing its limits.

passage: Pradeep Chacha leaned back. "Akash, when I was eleven, our colony had a rule for cricket: whoever breaks a window owns up. No running. One day my shot went straight through Mrs Kulkarni's glass. The others shouted, 'Run!' but I walked up and rang her bell. My knees were shaking. She was angry, but she said, 'At least you came.' When I walked back to the others, they looked at me differently. Next day, Bunty said, 'You kept the rule, man.' I felt taller that whole week, like I was the kind of person who does the right thing." Akash grinned. "Did you pay for it?" "Six months of pocket money."

qa.q: Whose window did young Pradeep break?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni's.

qa.q: How did young Pradeep feel when Bunty said "You kept the rule, man"?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated, like someone who does the right thing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what could young Pradeep have done if he felt too scared to go alone?
qa.a: The turning point was choosing to ring her bell instead of running; he could have asked a friend to come with him.

qa.q: How might Mrs Kulkarni have seen young Pradeep?
qa.a: She was angry about the window, but respected that he came to own up.

grounding: An uncle recalls feeling proud and validated after following the colony rule to own up to a broken window.

passage: Ten minutes left in the Class 7 test, and Bhavna Ma'am stepped out to answer the phone. The room buzzed. Someone whispered answers across the aisle. Anand kept his eyes on his paper, though his last answer was blank. "Psst, Anand, number 5?" "We said no talking in tests," Anand whispered back. "Everyone agreed." He felt his heart thumping. When Bhavna Ma'am returned, she looked around. "Who kept the rule?" A few raised hands, Anand's among them. "Thank you," she said. Anand sat straighter. His blank answer still bothered him, but he felt good.

qa.q: How many minutes were left in the test?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Bhavna Ma'am said "Thank you"?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated for keeping the rule, even with a blank answer.

qa.q: What could Bhavna Ma'am do to keep the class's agreement strong?
qa.a: She could remind everyone why they agreed on the rule and not leave the room during tests.

qa.q: How might the classmate who whispered see Anand's reply?
qa.a: They might feel annoyed or a little embarrassed at being reminded of the rule.

grounding: During a test, a boy keeps the agreed no-talking rule and feels validated when the teacher thanks those who did.

passage: In the Thane society, Sunday was waste-sorting day, and Irawati was proud of her job: checking the bins in their wing. Wet waste in green, dry in blue. When Kamal Uncle from the third floor tossed a plastic bag into the green bin, she said, "Uncle, that goes in blue. We all agreed at the meeting." He paused, then moved it. "Right you are." Irawati felt a glow. Then she saw her own brother drop a wrapper in green. "Arre! Even you?" Her mother laughed. "Rules for everyone, na?" Irawati moved the wrapper herself, smiling.

qa.q: What colour bin was for wet waste?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after Kamal Uncle moved the bag?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated, a glow of doing the right thing.

qa.q: How could Irawati make sure her reminders come across kindly?
qa.a: She could keep her tone friendly and help fix mistakes, as she did with her brother's wrapper.

qa.q: How might Kamal Uncle see being corrected by a child?
qa.a: He seems a little surprised but takes it well, agreeing that she's right.

grounding: A girl feels proud upholding her building's waste-sorting rule, even with her own family.

passage:
"Rashmi, you brought your phone?" Mehak whispered on the picnic bus.

"No. We all agreed, no phones this picnic."

"But Tanu brought hers."

"That's Tanu's choice. We voted."

At the lake, Tanu spent the whole time on her phone. Rashmi, Mehak and the others played frisbee and caught tadpoles.

On the way back, Ma'am said, "Thank you to everyone who kept our promise."

Rashmi sat up straighter. "See? It felt good to keep it."

Mehak nodded. "Even if Tanu didn't."

qa.q: What did the class agree about phones?
qa.a: They agreed no phones this picnic.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when Ma'am thanked the class?
qa.a: Rashmi felt proud and good about keeping the shared promise.

qa.q: How could Ma'am build on this feeling?
qa.a: She could involve children in making rules together, so they value keeping them.

qa.q: How might Tanu feel when Ma'am thanked the others?
qa.a: Tanu might feel a bit left out or embarrassed.

grounding: A girl feels proud and validated for keeping a class rule about phones on a picnic.

passage:
The Holi I was ten, our colony had one rule: no colour on anyone who says no.

Gargi, from the corner house, said no. She was wearing her school uniform because she was going for tuition.

My friend Bunty picked up a handful of green anyway. I grabbed his wrist. "She said no. That's the rule."

He was annoyed. "It's Holi!"

"Rules are for Holi too."

He dropped it. Later, Gargi waved at me from her gate.

I'm Pankaj, and I remember walking home feeling taller.

qa.q: What was the colony's rule?
qa.a: No colour on anyone who says no.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel walking home?
qa.a: Pankaj felt proud and good, like standing taller, for upholding the rule.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do that was right?
qa.a: He stopped Bunty and reminded him of the shared rule, protecting Gargi's choice.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel when she waved at Pankaj?
qa.a: Gargi likely felt grateful and respected.

grounding: A child remembers upholding a Holi rule to respect a girl's choice and feeling proud.

passage:
Badminton coach's note, winter tournament.

In the semi-final, Mahima's team won a point that the umpire didn't see was out. Mahima raised her hand. "It was out."

Her partner groaned. The opponent, Irfan, looked surprised.

The point was replayed, and Mahima's team lost it. But they won the match.

Afterwards Mahima said, "I didn't want to win because of a mistake. That's not how we play."

I told the team that honesty is part of the game. — Coach

qa.q: What did Mahima say about the point?
qa.a: She raised her hand and said, "It was out."

qa.q: How did Mahima feel about telling the truth?
qa.a: Mahima felt proud and right about upholding fair play, even though it cost a point.

qa.q: How did the coach support Mahima's choice?
qa.a: The coach told the team that honesty is part of the game.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel about Mahima's honesty?
qa.a: Irfan was surprised and probably respected her fair play.

grounding: A coach notes a girl upholding fair play and feeling validated by keeping to shared rules.

passage:
Dear Diary, 13 August
For Independence Day our class is running a treasure hunt, and we all promised not to open the clue envelopes early. Today Mridul tried to peek at the third clue in the staffroom corridor. I said, "We promised. It's not fair on everyone else." He rolled his eyes, but four others backed me up, and he put it back. Walking home I felt about ten feet tall, like the judge in a courtroom. Then I remembered I'd almost peeked at the first clue last week myself. I'm still glad I spoke up.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Mridul try to do in the staffroom corridor?
qa.a: Mridul tried to peek at the third clue.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel walking home?
qa.a: Sabina felt proud and in the right, "about ten feet tall", for upholding the class promise.

qa.q: How could Sabina's last thought help next time?
qa.a: Remembering that almost-peek keeps the pride humble, so Sabina can speak up firmly without judging Mridul too harshly.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel after four classmates backed Sabina?
qa.a: Mridul may feel embarrassed and outnumbered, perhaps a bit resentful at being called out.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated for upholding a rule the whole class agreed on before Independence Day.
